Meeting called to order by Brother Bridgman at 9:20 A. M.
Minutes of the preceding meeting were read, and after corrections, ap

A telegram was read from the Beta stating that Brothers Frederick Potts
and Thomas Sargent were coming as the delegates of that Chapter.

Committee on New Business submitted the following resolution:
Resolved: That the ninety-first year Convention of the Psi Upsilon Fra
ternity recommend that the Chapters set aside annually a sum of two dollars
($2.00) per member to be accumulated until the Psi Upsilon Centennial in 1938.
Said fund to be expended for a fitting memorial to be determined by the Exec
utive Council and the Convention.

It was moved, seconded and passed that this resolution be adopted.

Appendix A.
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION OF THE EXECUTIVE COUNCIL TO THE

1924 CONVENTION.

At this Convention of the Ninety-first Year of our Fraternity, the Exec
utive Council extends its congratulations and felicitations to the chapters upon
their preservation of the high ideals and excellent personnel o four Fraternity.
The reports received from the various members of the Council who have visited
different chapters over the past year are most gratifying and show the Fra
ternity to be in a prosperous condition.
Eecords :
. The compiling of facts for the supplement to the generad cata
logue has demonstrated that some of the chapters are becoming rather careless
as regards their records, and the Council feels that some arrangement should

be made by which the Fraternity should be certain every year that the records
of each chapter are in good form. There should be an alumnus master of the
rolls and two undergraduates for each chapter.

The Council recommends that the Convention empower the Council to ap

point a national master of the rolls whose duty shall be the continual main
tenance of the accuracy of our catalogue.
Scholarship: While in our last communication the Council set forth the

necessity for
haising the standard of
scholarship, we would again emphasize
and hope that the committee will devise ways and means by which this may

be obtained. scholarship standing of Psi U in the various institutions
The
where we have chapters is none too gratifying and something must be done to

place every chapter of Psi U among the upper half in scholarship ranking.
Diamond: Eeport of the Executive Council's Committee on The Diamond.'
having recognized that the value of the restored
The Executive Couneil
Diamond has been demonstrated to the entire fraternity, unanimously decided
that the publication should now be placed on a permanent basis.

Therefore, the Executive Council at its meeting on March 6th, 1924, ap
pointed Brothers Houston, Babst and Corcoran, as committee to study the
present status of The Diamond and to report to the Council its suggestions as
to means arid methods desirable to be presented to the Annual Convention for
a
permanent basis of supportfor the continued publication of The Diamond.
The Committee begs to report as follows :
1st. The Committe considers the revival of The Diamond now in its fourth

year an outstanding success and widely appreciated by the under

graduates and alumni as evidenced by its 2500 subscribers.

12

2nd. That in its judgment The Diamond merits the support of the Annual
Convention and of permanent financing along lines found successful
with similar publications and briefly as follows :
a. By the establishment of life subscriptions for $10.00, to be in
cluded by each chapter in its initiation fee, and by a similar sub

scription by each sophomore, junior and esnior as of October 1st,
1924.

b. By voluntary life subscriptions of $10.00 to present alumni sub
.

scribers and as absolute terms to all other alumni as of October

1st, 1924.
3rd. Such a plan is estimated to yield a capital publication fund of at

least$12,000 by October 1st, 1925, which will be added to each year
by subsequent life subscriptions of initiates and alumni thus provid
ing a growing endowment that will insure the permanency of The
Diamond.

4th. It is recommended that the publication be established in corporate
form and that the endowment funds be invested under such authority
as the Convention may designate.
Note of Explanation It will be necessary to buiW the capital fund from

the subscriptions from alumni and the undergraduates excepting
freshmen who make payment in 1924. Thereafter, the necessary
portion of the sum received each year from the freshmen will be
available to pay for the running expenses until the capital is sufficient.

Eespectfully submitted,
Eael D. Babst,
Herbert S. Houston,
E. Bourke Corcoran.

Election to the Council: The Council would call attention to the fact
that the terms of President Herbert L. Bridgman, Gamma '66, and Secretary
Emmett Hay Naylor, Zeita '09, expiire at this Convention. Therefore, it will be
necessary for the Convention to elect two members to the Execuive Council.

Necrology: Since the last Convention among prominent alumni that Psi

Upsilon has lost are Brothers James M. Gilbert, Pi '75, member of the Exec
utive Council from 1882-1883, and Austin M. Poole, Delta '87, member of the
Executive Council from 1909-1923.

The Council deeply regrets the passing of these alumni and active Psi U's
as well as the death of other Psi U 's which have been reported in The Diamond,
that being the method which the Council feels is much more prompt and thor
ough than the annual notification in this communication.

13

Chapter Initiates : In considering candidates for election to Psi
Upsilon,
if there is any question as to a man's home environment, social
standing, etc..
the chapter should communicate at once with the chapter nearest the man's
home asking that chapter to look up and report on all facts as regards the
candidate. A chapter should seriously hesitate about initiating
any man who
is objected to by another chapter.

Expulsion : The Council takes occasion again to call the chapters ' atten
tion to Article VI, Section 8, of the Constitution and by-laws, and, in addition
to this provision, would indicate that there must be notice given to the man to
be expelled, of the chapter's intention to act, with charges and specifications
clearly stated, and a hearing in defense must be held. Grounds for expulsions
should be such as are set forth in the Constitution and by-laws, or such other

grounds which are clearly destructive of and a violation of the fundamental
objects of the Fraternity. The Council, in addition, would advise a moderation
in the use of the penalty of expulsion as in many cases suspension will often
better serve the purpose.

Songs : As Psi Upsilon is chiefly a society o fthe spirit and as songs are

the vocal expression of that spirit, the Council would urge a greater respect for,
and more singing of, our Fraternity songs. Care should be taken that these
songs not sung to various tempos but should all be sung with dignity and
are

reverence at the metronome time indicated at the
top of each song in the official
song book. After an undergraduate becomes an alumnus he
appreciates that
one of the most beautiful memories he has of Psi U and of the strongest
one

bonds which binds him to our
Fraternity is his knowledge of, and reverence
for, our various songs.
Petitions: In accordance with the vote of the last convention, the Coun

chapters was taken on the petition of Pi
cil wishes to report that a vote of the

Upsilon Society of the University of Kansas, and that vote is as follows : For
10; Against 16.
The Council is again in receipt of another petition from the Pi Upsilon
Society of the University of Kansas whieh it respectfully submits to the An
nual Convention.

The Council wishes also to call again to the attention of the Fraternity
a petition which has been received from the Wranglers of Northwestern Uni
versity.
Conduct at Conventions : In view of the restrictions as set forth by the

Constitution of the United States supplemented by the Volstead Act, and the
regulations as enforced by local authorities, the Council would not only urge,
but, in so far as lies within its power, would insist that all brothers, both under-

14

graduates and alumni, at any convention, refrain from the use in any way what
soever of intoxicating liquors. It must be remembered that any indiscretion
reflects not only on the Fraternity but especially on the chapter where the Con
vention is being held.

Graduation: The attached table shows the relative standing of the active
classes of each chapter of the Fraternity.
The Council regrets that in many instances chapters show a decided falling
off in the delegations between freshmen and senior years, not so much due appa
rently to low scholarship as to leaving the college or university to enter business.
.Again the Council would emphasize that a chapter can best be judged by
the size and standing of its senior delegation and that no man, no matter how
good he may be, should be initiated into Psi Upsilon unless there is a reasonable
assurance of his graduation. Four years is all to short for a man to be imbued
with the spirit and the tradition of Psi Upsilon and he can reflect no better
credit upon the Fraternity than to graduate with his delegation with scholastic
honors.
Eespectfully and fraternally submitted,
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL,
E. H. Naylor,
Secretary-Recorder.
Approved AprU 26, 1924.

REPORT OP THE TREASURER, 1924
The last Annual Report of the Treasurer showed among Expenditures from
the General Fund, an inventory charge-off of $351.37, representing the sheets
of 500 unbound song books which in their unsalable form represented no real
cash asset value.

During the past year these have been compiled and bound, and the words
and music of the Rho Owl Song have been added ; in the attached Eeport of the
Treasurer will be found under Income Accrued to the General Fund an item of

$725.00, under Adjustment of Inventory, covering write-up of 500 copies of

song books rebound and salable. This amount together with the cost of com

pilation and rebinding $275.00, charged to Song Book Account during the year,
gives a total of $1,000, the sales value of 500 copies. Both song books and
catalogues are carried at sale value of $2.00 per copy.
During the year the remaining copies of the old song'books have been sold
and 85 copies of the newly bound edition, leaving a balance on hand of 415
copies.
The write-offs, under Expenditures, of the General and Convention Funds,
referring to the Beta Chapter and amounting to $144,50 and $25.50 respectively,
are in accordance with resolution passed at last year 's Convention, these
amounts representing the accrued tax for 1922 as pertaining to members of the
Senior delegation of that year.

Eespectfully and fraternally submitted,
Walter T. Collins,
Treasurer.
April 17, 1924.
